transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-20 14:00 PT
Duration: ~72 minutes
Recording id: ff-20261120-amp-001
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood Platform), Priya (Amphora Head ML Infra), Liam (SRE), Aisha (CTO), Samir (Infra)

Summary block (auto): Amphora seeing sporadic GPU stalls after KV cache fills and during high-concurrency bursts. Suspect: async stream synchronization edge case when mixed-quant models and prefetch overlap; possibility of driver-level retry causing stream hang or kernel queue stall.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll keep this focused — Diego is going to drive the deep dive and then we'll land on concrete next steps. Priya, quick context?
[00:14] Priya: yeah, thanks. We've been running Redwood Dedicated in our VPC for two months, most traffic is inference for search rerank. Last two weeks we started seeing tail latency spikes, sometimes full request timeouts. When we dug in the GPU was stuck, not OOM exactly, but kernels never return, and the process is alive.
[00:33] Liam: to add we're seeing this on two different instance types, both A100s but different drivers. We thought it might be fragmentation or OOM, but memory usage is within expected bounds; it's more like a synchronization hang.
[00:47] Diego: ok, thanks — so queueing question: are you running mixed-quant models here? int8 on some shards and fp16 elsewhere?
[00:56] Samir: yes, we have an int8 quantized variant we use for high-throughput routes. Most of the traffic is batched, but we also see large prefix KV cache fills when customers do long-context loads.
[01:12] Diego: got it — common pattern that can stress the KV cache prefetch and asynchronous copy paths. Our hypothesis is there's a timing window where cudaMemcpyAsync + kernel launches on different streams get out of order after a stream event wait, causing a deadlock-like stall if a kernel waits on an event that never signals because prefetch got batched/canceled.
[01:34] Priya: right and the timeouts are intermittent, like 20s to 90s, sometimes a subsequent request clears the stuck GPU, sometimes it needs a driver reset.
[01:45] Aisha: and to be clear, this only started after we enabled aggressive KV prefetching and tightened batch thresholds — before that, largely stable.
[01:56] Lena: I want to call out the interaction with quantization: int8 kernels sometimes use custom fused kernels and different launch configs. If a fused kernel hits a corner case (e.g., misaligned tensor or padded dim) it may spin on a device-side loop or hit an assert that doesn't surface cleanly to the host, therefore the host waits forever on stream completion.
[02:16] Diego: exactly. Also driver versions differ in how they report a stuck kernel; older drivers occasionally return without obvious NVML errors.
[02:24] Maya: can we pull logs? Samir — do you have any dmesg, kernel oops, or nvml logs from a host that saw the hang?
[02:31] Samir: we do. I uploaded a short excerpt to the chat — there's a repeated 'NVRM: GPU HANG' line in one host and a second host shows 'cuda: stream timeout' entries but no full kernel stack.
[02:49] Diego: good. We'll need full kernel stack traces and the nv-hostengine logs. Also please collect cuda-smi --loop 1 output around the timeframe and nvprof/nvtx traces if possible.
[03:01] Liam: note we can't put production hosts into heavy profiling for long. We'd prefer a repro on a staging cluster that mirrors the prefetch/batch pattern.
[03:12] Diego: understood; we'll create a lightweight reproducer that simulates the KV warm path and mixed int8/fp16 launches. It will use NVTX regions so you can run it briefly in staging.
[03:24] Priya: good. A few observed artifacts: (1) long-run queue backlog on stream 2, (2) high PCIe copy pending count, (3) occasional soft OOM messages before the hang. Sometimes the hang correlates with long sequence length spikes.
[03:41] Diego: those are helpful. The soft OOMs might be memory fragmentation from repeated cache churn combined with batching. But the stream backlog pattern points at synchronization order inversion — particularly if we use separate copy and compute streams and rely on event ordering without strong fencing.
[03:58] Aisha: from an ops perspective, what's the immediate mitigation? We need graceful degradation so a single stuck request doesn't take down a whole GPU.
[04:07] Lena: two quick levers: (A) introduce a user-space watchdog that cancels long-running requests and issues a soft reset to per-request context; (B) fallback routing — if a GPU shows >X ms stall, route to a less-quantized variant or to another region. We can provide a config snippet for Dedicated and Private deployments.
[04:30] Maya: we'll attach that as a patch. Also, what about retry semantics — do we do automatic retry on stuck calls? That can make it worse if retries queue up.
[04:40] Diego: correct — our recommendation is to not spin retries aggressively. Use exponential backoff and decrement batch credits when a request is retried, and prefer model-variant fallback rather than blind retry. We'll share the recommended semantics.
[04:55] Priya: logging question — how do we distinguish device-side hang from host-level stall? Some of our traces show the host still reporting kernel running but no nvml error.
[05:06] Diego: NVTX/trace + nvprof timeline is critical; device-side hangs often show kernels consuming SMs with no forward progress in profiler counters. A host-level stall without kernel churn may indicate a blocked host thread or stalled stream. Also look for blocked async memcopies (cudaMemcpyAsync stuck in uncompleted state).
[05:28] Liam: driver versions: we're on 520.x on one fleet, 535.x on another. Any known regressions?
[05:34] Diego: there have been fixes around stream event handling in later 53x drivers. We'll include a compatibility matrix. That said, don't upgrade blindly; reproduce first and test driver rollout in staging.
[05:47] Aisha: what about kernel-level preemption? If a long kernel blocks, preemption may not be enabled depending on SM config; does Redwood have preemption-friendly kernels?
[05:58] Lena: we aim for fast, cooperative kernels for attention and kv-cache ops. But fused int8 kernels can run longer; adding small yields (grid-level checks) can help but at throughput cost. Tradeoff to discuss.
[06:12] Priya: can quantization make this worse? I.e., int8 fused paths being less forgiving?
[06:18] Diego: yes — int8 paths often have custom code paths and will behave differently under misaligned inputs or extreme sequence lengths. For repro we'll test identical inputs across int8 and fp16 to see divergence.
[06:30] Samir: one more data point: when we disabled prefetch on a subset of hosts the incidence dropped by ~60%. That suggests prefetch/copy overlap is a big factor.
[06:41] Diego: good telemetry. Reproducer will toggle the prefetch rate and batch size to hit the same window.
[06:47] Maya: let's walk through the reproduce plan and required artifacts. Diego?
[06:52] Diego: reproduce plan: 1) lightweight script that spawns N concurrent clients, issues a mix of long-context and short-context requests to warm KV cache; 2) instrument with NVTX around prefetch and compute; 3) collect nvprof/nvtx timeline plus cuda-smi loop and dmesg; 4) run on staging A100 with both driver versions. We'll post the script and run commands in the shared doc.
[07:18] Priya: what about fallback — if we detect a stuck GPU how should our router behave? Pause routing to that GPU and spread load?
[07:26] Lena: router should implement graceful drain with a cooldown window. If a host shows > X consecutive long-tail stalls, mark it degraded and stop sending new long-context requests; allow short fast paths with lower memory footprint. We'll share thresholds based on our prod signals.
[07:41] Liam: do we have any suggestion to change batch sizing dynamically to avoid hitting the window?
[07:47] Diego: yes, dynamic batch caps based on in-flight copy bytes and KV cache utilization. If the cache is busy and prefetch queue high, reduce max batch length and prefer more frequent flushes. This reduces throughput but stabilizes latency.
[07:59] Aisha: ok, so immediate action: (1) reproduce in staging, (2) collect traces, (3) apply watchdog + cooldown prototype, (4) test fallback to fp16 variant.
[08:11] Maya: agreed. We'll capture action items. Any final clarifying Qs?
[08:16] Priya: one last ask — can Redwood SE include a sample NVTX instrumentation plan? We rarely use NVTX in prod so a template would help.
[08:24] Diego: yes we'll include a simple NVTX insert around prefetch, copy, compute, and event waits; also how to interpret the timeline.
[08:33] Samir: note on private deployment: our security team requires any reproducer artifacts to be runnable entirely within our VPC — no external data. We will coordinate on that.
[08:40] Maya: understood. We'll make the reproducer self-contained.
[08:44] -- meeting wrap, recap of next steps and owners --
